old_title: Iran war live: Trump 'low-keying it' as Tehran demands compensation to reopen Hormuz
new_title: Iran war latest: Trump claims control of Hormuz as he demands Iran pay for US deaths
old_text:
US president Donald Trump has said the US is "low-keying it" with Iran as talks to end their war and reopen shipping through the Strait of Hormuz appeared to have stalled.
"We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," he told Axios.
Tehran, meanwhile, has set out a series of demands that it says the US must meet before it will sign off on a deal with Oman to partially open up the Strait, including the payment of compensation for war damages.
The head of Iran's supreme national security council, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, said the strait will remain shut until the US meet six conditions, including a permanent end to the war and aggression against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen, and Iraq.
It comes as the US is pushing for defence companies to "dramatically" accelerate weapons production as the Iran war drains through their missile supplies, according to a memo obtained by The Washington Post.
Watch: Houthis release video claiming ballistic missile and drone attack on Saudi Arabia
Iran says deal in 'final stages' - but reiterates conditions before opening Hormuz
Tehran said on Sunday that a new deal with Oman defining new shipping lanes in the Strait of Hormuz was in its final stages - but reiterated that the waterway would only reopen if the US meets several conditions.
Agreement between Iran and Oman over the strait, which separates the two countries, is seen as vital to a wider deal to end the war.
One of the conditions being demanded by Tehran is compensation from the US following the launch of its war, alongside Israel, on 28 February.
The secretary of Iran's top national security body, Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, listed other demands including ending US threats against Iran, stopping aggression against Iran and its Lebanese, Palestinian, Yemeni and Iraqi allies, lifting a blockade and sanctions on Iran and freeing Iranian assets.
Bulletin | Trump says US is 'only semi-negotiating' as Iran talks stall
Here's everything you need to know in just five lines with The Independent's Bulletin:
Recap: UAE oil tanker attacked by missile in Strait of Hormuz
As we reported last night, the United Arab Emirates condemned an Iranian missile attack on its carrier as it passed through the Strait of Hormuz, accusing Tehran of "acts of piracy".
State news agency WAM initially reported ADNOC as saying one of its vessels had been targeted by a missile early on Saturday and that the situation was under control.
The UAE Foreign Ministry later condemned what it called "the hostile Iranian attack" on an ADNOC vessel.
Neither statement gave details on the tanker, its cargo or possible damage. No injuries were reported.
The ministry said the attack violated a UN Security Council resolution on freedom of navigation and accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of "acts of piracy" by targeting commercial shipping and using the waterway as a tool of economic pressure.
Yemen's Houthis attack Saudi refinery
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis say they have struck the Jazan refinery in Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi energy ministry said a fire had broken out at the refinery but was later extinguished with no injuries and authorities were dealing with the incident, without giving a cause.
The Houthis used a drone to target the refinery, military spokesperson Yahya Saree posted on X. They had struck Aramco sites before in Jazan, which processes 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day in southwestern Saudi Arabia. They had also hit Yanbu on the Red Sea.
The Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last month, citing what they said was a Saudi siege on them, an allegation Riyadh denies.
In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis carried out missile and drone strikes on the Yemeni Red Sea port city of Mocha.
The port, controlled by the Aden-based government, is close to the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait, which links the southern Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Should it be closed, Saudi Arabia would be deprived of an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
Houthis strike ships at oil chokepoints
Iranian strikes on Strait of Hormuz shipping have been coupled with increased attacks by its Yemen-based allies, the Houthi rebels, who have targeted ships at another oil chokepoint on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula between the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
The Houthis also declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea last month in response to what they said was a Saudi siege on them in Yemen, an allegation denied by Riyadh, which backs Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The Yemeni rebel group said they had attacked Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery on Sunday, two days after the kingdom signed a defence pact with Sunni Muslim allies Turkey and Pakistan in response to growing regional instability from the US-Israeli war on Shi'ite Iran.
The Saudi energy ministry said a fire had broken out at the refinery but was later extinguished with no injuries, without giving a cause.
Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan said the new alliance was not directed against Iran or any other country, but rather served as a general pledge to support security.
Fighting has escalated between the Houthis and government forces in Yemen, with the Yemeni military on Monday saying seven people including military personnel and civilians were killed in a Houthi attack on the Red Sea port city of Mocha.
Air defences intercepted and shot down 11 Houthi drones that participated in the attack, the military said.
Yemeni military says Houthi attack on Mocha kills 7, wounds 30
The Yemeni military said seven people, including military personnel and civilians, were killed and 30 others wounded in a Houthi attack on the Red Sea port city of Mocha.
"Four members of the armed forces and three civilians have been killed, and 30 others injured," the Yemeni military said in a statement early on Monday. Air defences intercepted and shot down 11 Houthi drones that participated in the attack, the military said.
Footage shown by Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV showed the launch of several ballistic missiles and drones, which Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on Telegram targeted Saudi troop concentrations and weapons depots.
The Yemeni military said the Houthi attacks had also targeted residential neighbourhoods in Mocha.
Iran replaces top security chief as Tehran denies direct US talks on ending war
Iran has appointed a senior commander from its powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps as its new top security official, in a major reshuffle that comes as Tehran denies holding direct negotiations with Washington to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Mohsen Rezaei, previously an adviser to supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, will take over as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, a spokesperson for president Masoud Pezeshkian said late on Sunday.
He replaces Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who resigned from the post and will now serve as a political adviser to Khamenei.
Zolghadr had held the role since March, when his predecessor, Ali Larijani, was killed in an Israeli air strike.
The change at the heart of Iran's security establishment comes amid competing accounts over efforts to bring the conflict to an end.
Foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was not engaged in direct talks with the United States over ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, despite US officials claiming that the two sides were close to reaching an agreement.
Israel and Hamas disagree over timings in Trump's plan
Donald Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough in his plan to end the war, to which both Israel and Hamas agreed, with Israeli forces withdrawing as Hamas disarms and an International Stabilisation Force working with a new Palestinian police force to secure the enclave.
But complications have swiftly emerged with questions over the plan's timeline."Israel does not accept the 15-point document," Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said at the start of a meeting with cabinet ministers.
The military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed ... it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry", he said. Netanyahu made similar remarks in a social media post on Tuesday and Israeli officials have said reservations have been shared with Washington.
He added that Israel was in talks with the United States on the plan. "They (the US) have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us and we know how to stand firm against these things," Netanyahu said.
Basem Naim, a senior Hamas official, told Reuters on Sunday that the group remained committed to the roadmap agreed in Cairo 10 days ago.
"We expect the mediators and the US guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," he said.
Netanyahu says Trump's new Gaza plan is unacceptable
Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu restated his rejection of Donald Trump's latest Gaza plan in televised remarks to his right-wing government on Sunday, even as Israel's military has effectively halted attacks in the territory under pressure from the US president.
Netanyahu is struggling in the polls as he seeks re-election at a vote due on 27 October but is caught between far-right ministers angered by concessions in Gaza and his key military backer, Trump, who wants progress toward ending the conflict there with a new 15-point roadmap. Israel has scaled back attacks in Gaza since Monday, when Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza envoy for Trump's Board of Peace that oversees the ceasefire, met with Netanyahu.
A source familiar with Israel's position said it had agreed that the military would only act against what it perceives as immediate threats in Gaza and no longer carry out targeted assassinations as it had been doing on a near-daily basis. Mladenov said on Sunday that discussions on the new roadmap were ongoing.
new_text:
Donald Trump says the US Navy has cleared mines from the Strait of Hormuz and now has "100 per cent" control of the key waterway, which Iran says will remain closed until Washington meets its demands.
Trump told reporters in the Oval Office: "It's open now," claiming the US was "the only one that has control of the Strait of Hormuz right now".
Trump, meanwhile, demanded war compensation from Iran on Monday in a shocking reversal of the six-point ultimatum presented to Washington as Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran's top security official said earlier that they would allow traffic to pass through the key channel only once the US meets six terms, including "payment in full" for damage inflicted during the war.
But Trump snubbed the proposal in a message on Truth Social, saying: "It is an interesting idea because now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran," Trump said, adding: "I have instructed my representatives to put this firmly into any, and all, future negotiations."
Trump secretly switched planes to leave Turkey due to Iran assassination threat
US president Donald Trump was secretly transported away from last month's Nato summit in Ankara, Turkey, using a secondary military plane while an elaborate deception made it seem he was aboard Air Force One, according to a report published by The Washington Post on Monday.
The newspaper reported that the covert movement was triggered by an assassination threat from Iran targeting Mr Trump. Reporters and several White House personnel were left believing they were travelling on the same aircraft as the president as his return journey to Washington commenced following the annual gathering of Nato leaders.
The newspaper based its account on reviewed documentation, a US official aware of the operation and another individual familiar with the president's travel arrangements.
Who are Iran's new wartime commanders?
Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has appointed six senior commanders to key military and security posts, reshaping the wartime leadership after several top commanders were killed.
The appointments came a day after former IRGC chief Mohsen Rezaee was named secretary of the Supreme National Security Council.
- Ali Abdollahi: Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces, overseeing coordination across the military.
- Kioumars Heydari: Deputy Chief of Staff.
- Ahmad Vahidi: New IRGC commander, tasked with boosting deterrence and readiness for "powerful offensive operations".
- Mostafa Izadi: Vahidi's deputy, responsible for operational readiness.
- Ali Ozmaei: New IRGC Navy commander, a key role amid tensions around the Strait of Hormuz.
- Hossein Taeb: New Basij commander, focusing on mobilisation and domestic intelligence. Basij is Iran's paramilitary volunteer militia within the IRGC.
British couple jailed in Iran over espionage end their hunger strike
British couple Craig and Lindsay Foreman, who have been jailed in Iran on widely criticised espionage charges, have ended hunger strikes lasting 93 and 84 days respectively.
The East Sussex couple, who deny the charges, were arrested in January last year while travelling by motorcycle from Europe to Australia and sentenced to 10 years in prison in February.
Craig Foreman's sentence was later reportedly extended after he spoke to the media.
They began the hunger strike in May after prison authorities stopped them from contacting their families.
They agreed to end it after guards promised they could resume direct contact, though their family said Monday that contact had not yet been restored.
Oil prices rise as US-Iran negotiations over Strait of Hormuz seem to stall
Oil prices rose as US-Iran negotiations over reopening the Strait of Hormuz stalled. Brent climbed to $88 a barrel and US crude to $82.45, both their highest levels since 31 July, after a roughly 5 per cent jump on Monday.
The latest escalation came after Donald Trump rejected Iran's terms for reopening the strait and instead demanded compensation from Tehran, raising fears that the crucial shipping route will remain disrupted.
He later wrote on Truth Social: "Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!"
Chuck Schumer attacks Trump over Iran war
US Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer has called Donald Trump's handling of the Iran war a "complete and total failure".
"Donald Trump got us into an illegal war, is losing his illegal war, and has no way out of his illegal war," Schumer wrote on X.
"His lack of strategy, discipline, and any ability to seriously negotiate is endangering our troops and raising prices for everyday Americans," he said.
"Trump's leadership is a complete and total failure. We must end this war and begin to repair the damage he has wrought," he added.
Trump demands war reparations from Iran after Tehran called for compensation
Donald Trump has said he will demand war reparations from Iran for the deaths and injuries of US soldiers and civilians over decades.
He made the demand after Iranian negotiators called for compensation for the destruction caused by the war, which has killed thousands and severely damaged Iran's military and economy.
Trump wrote on Truth Social: "Now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by Gen Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat.
"Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protesters that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months."
Catch up: Trump says 'it always works out' as plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz stalls
Donald Trump has declared that it "always works out" as he said the US will scale down the intensity of its efforts to reopen shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Talks to end their war and reopen shipping through the Strait of Hormuz appeared to have stalled, after Tehran demanded a series of conditions, including the payment of compensation, before it reopens the waterway.
"We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," he told Axios. "It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game."
Tehran is in negotiations with Oman to partially open up the Strait, but set out six conditions the US must meet, including a permanent end to the war and aggression against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen, and Iraq.
Trump used elaborate ruse to fly out of Turkey following summit because of Iran threat - report
Donald Trump secretly switched from Air Force One to a smaller military jet after last month's Nato summit in Turkey amid an Iranian assassination threat, The Washington Post reported.
After publicly boarding an older Air Force One, Trump was reportedly moved via an airport catering truck to an Air Force C-32A and flown to the UK, while journalists were led to believe he remained on Air Force One.
The US has not independently confirmed the report.
"As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement.
During a gaggle with reporters aboard the aircraft, Trump was asked directly if there was any credible threats on Air Force One by Iran, according to the Associated Press.
"Well, I have a threat all the time. I'm number one on their list before you," Trump said. He added to the travelling reporters, "But if I go, you go."
Iran president says supreme leader shared message of 'unity and cohesion'
Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian has said that Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had a message of "unity and cohesion" during a recent meeting that lasted seven hours.
Pezeshkian said Khamenei, who hasn't made an appearance since becoming supreme leader, was in perfect health.
On Monday, Khamenei's office announced several key appointments, including the selection of a former wartime commander and veteran political insider to lead the country's highest security body.
